prompt.en: Two nearby portable Yagis point their booms at each other, but one has upright elements and the other has level elements. Which change aligns their polarizations while keeping their aim?

text.en: Rotate one antenna about its boom by a quarter turn.

feedback.en: A quarter turn changes that element orientation by 90 degrees, aligning it with the other antenna.

text.en: Rotate both antennas about their booms by a quarter turn.

feedback.en: Both orientations change together, so they remain perpendicular to each other.

text.en: Rotate one antenna about its boom by a half turn.

feedback.en: A half turn leaves the element axis with the same upright or level orientation, so the mismatch remains.

text.en: Turn both booms in azimuth while keeping one set of elements upright and the other level.

feedback.en: Changing compass aim does not align the element orientations, and it can reduce directional gain toward each other.

explanation.en: Keep aim and element orientation separate. Rotating a single antenna about its boom can change polarization without changing the main pointing direction.

prompt.en: Two dipoles cut to the same dimensions resonate at different frequencies after installation. One is close to metal siding. What should be investigated first?

text.en: Small cutting errors, treating the first-cut dimensions as a finished installed design.

feedback.en: Cutting accuracy is worth checking, but the nearby metal is a known difference between installations. A first-cut estimate is not a finished installed design.

text.en: The effect of nearby objects and end conditions on electrical length.

feedback.en: Equal physical cuts can behave differently in different surroundings.

text.en: Coax length, treating it as the main adjustment for the wire's own resonance.

feedback.en: Cable length can alter the impedance seen at the radio under mismatch. It does not resolve the effect of nearby metal on the wire's resonance.

text.en: Conductor diameter, treating equal wire size as enough to disregard the siding.

feedback.en: Equal wire diameter does not remove environmental effects. Nearby objects can still alter the electrical behaviour of the installed dipole.

explanation.en: Keep the model limits in view when applying a wire-length estimate to real installations.

prompt.en: A calculator entry uses 300 / 0.92 to estimate wavelength at 0.92 GHz. Which repair makes the shortcut valid?

text.en: Keep the entry and label the result metres because all frequency prefixes work.

feedback.en: The 300 shortcut requires MHz. A GHz number makes the result a thousand times too large.

text.en: Multiply the result by 1 000 because GHz is a larger unit.

feedback.en: That moves the answer in the wrong direction. Higher frequency gives a shorter wavelength.

text.en: Convert to 920 MHz, then calculate 300 / 920 ≈ 0.326 m.

feedback.en: Converting GHz to MHz gives the correct input unit for this free-space shortcut.

text.en: Use 143 / 0.92 because it already includes the GHz conversion.

feedback.en: 143 is a practical dipole factor with MHz input, not a conversion for GHz.

explanation.en: Units are part of a formula. The free-space wavelength shortcut uses metres and megahertz together.
